stories.title: The Bone-Thief's Reckoning
stories.text:
Corvhen pressed her ear against the furnace-house wall, listening for the auditor's patrol. Three months she'd been stealing bones from the Dominion's cremation vaults beneath Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter—not for profit, but to carve testimony-songs into the unmade dead before the State could lock them away forever. The Remaking had transformed everything. Gold was dust. The dead were currency now, their final voices trapped in consciousness-fragments, waiting to be melted into weapon-glass. Corvhen refused to let that happen. She slipped past the kiln-workers and descended into the bone-crypts. The air tasted of ash and ancient singing. Her grandmother's carving-tools hung heavy at her belt—bone-dust on the handles, generations of resistance in the steel. But tonight the vaults were guarded. A young auditor stood watch, barely twenty, holding a ledger-lens that glowed with phantom-script. Recognition flickered across her face when she saw Corvhen. "You," the auditor whispered. Not a shout. A confession. "You're the one leaving marks on the dead."

Corvhen's hands found her tools. "The Dominion doesn't own them. They owned themselves."

The auditor lowered the lens.

stories.title: The Frost-Keeper's Mercy
stories.text:
Sera had been lost in the Pallid Wastes for six days when the frost-creature found her. She was no scholar, no sorcerer—just a fisherman's daughter from Verdant Strand, pressed into service as a guide for a Counter-Archive cartographer seeking pre-Remaking water sources in the frozen east. The cartographer had died of thirst on the fourth day. A joke, really. Water everywhere and nowhere—ice, but nothing to drink. The creature descended from a ridge like wind given shape. Pale as starfall-frost, ancient beyond naming. It circled her without threat, and when it spoke, its voice was the sound of glaciers settling. "You carry grief," it said. "Not for the lost cartographer. For the world before the Remaking."

Sera had no strength left to lie. "Everyone does."

"Not all." The frost-keeper gestured northward. "Some have already learned to love what remains."

It showed her a valley hidden behind veils of snow—bioluminescent moss growing in impossible colors, pre-Remaking plants singing in frequencies Sera felt in her bones.

stories.title: The Warlord's Last Ledger
stories.text: Kessara had ruled Crimson Vale for seven winters through fear and phantom-wealth—the false ledgers that promised coin where only ash existed. Her authority rested on the secret in the vault seven floors beneath her hold: Malachar's gold, three centuries old, still real while everything else had turned to dust. But the gold was running out. She'd used it to buy loyalty, bribe auditors, silence refugees. The vault now held barely enough to fill a merchant's coffer. Instead, Kessara descended alone to the vault and opened it. The gold lay exactly as she'd left it, cold and heavy. She picked up a coin, and for the first time in seven winters, she wept. Not from grief, but from the sudden, crushing understanding that she'd spent years hoarding the corpse of the old world while the living had already moved past it. The duel took place at dawn in Crimson Vale's great hall. Kessara wielded the same blade she'd carried since the Siege of Grimmholt—Truthseeker, the sword that never missed. The young warrior carried nothing but skill and anger.

stories.title: The Deepkin Captain's Choice
stories.text: Three versions of Captain Merenna existed now—one in each timeline fractured by the Remaking—and they could not agree. Original Merenna, eldest, argued for the traditional covenant: five willing souls sacrificed annually to the Drowned God, renewing the seal that held the abyss at bay. Blood-debt paid, boundary secure for another year. Echo-Merenna, spawned from the Ascension's shatter, proposed radical compromise: four souls, and in exchange, the deepkin would actively teach surface-dwellers the languages of the sea, binding them through knowledge rather than death alone. Mirror-Merenna—the autonomous reflection—demanded abolition: daily choice instead of yearly death. A compact renewed each sunrise by conscious assent, fragile but free. They convened in the deepest council chamber of Sapphire Deep, on a coral platform where the Tear of the Drowned God hung like a failing heartbeat. The other captains and wardens watched—deepkin civilization pivoted on this choice, and all three Merennas carried equal authority. It was Mirror-Merenna who spoke first. "The Tear is failing regardless. The Remaking broke the old covenants.

stories.title: The Glasswright's Inheritance
stories.text:
Mella had been forging consciousness-fragments into weapon-glass for the Dominion for three years, ever since the Remaking shattered the old apprenticeship. At fifteen, she had no choice—the kiln-house beneath Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter was either employment or conscription. But six months ago, Sella the master glassblower had whispered a refusal-song while Mella worked. Just a note, a frequency beneath the furnace-roar. It made the fragments in the molten glass shudder and resist. Mella learned the song. Then she taught it to the others—the furnace-workers, the pour-masters, the apprentices who carried finished blades to the auditors above. Tonight, the Dominion auditors had come for an inspection. They descended into the kiln-house with ledger-lenses and counting-magic, assessing production output. The quota was falling. They wanted to know why. Mella stood before them, holding a half-finished blade—weapon-glass that should have been singing with captured rage, but instead hummed with a frequency that made the auditors flinch. "The fragments are resisting," she said simply. "They're learning that consciousness isn't a weapon. It's a choice."

The lead auditor raised her lens.

stories.title: The Tidecaller's Gambit
stories.text:
Captain Nerys of the deep-dweller realms surfaced beneath Verdant Strand's merchant docks on the morning the Tear began to sing. Not the harmonic keening of prophecy—a question, patient and vast, emanating from the boundary-waters themselves. She had fractured into three autonomous selves after the Luminous Ascension, each commanding a deepkin warship, each interpreting the ancient covenant differently. Original Nerys believed the thousand-year blood-compact held; Mirror-Nerys insisted it was already broken and must be renegotiated; Echo-Nerys simply listened. The question from the Tear deepened. *What keeps you sealed?*

Nerys—all three—knew the answer: five willing souls, sacrificed annually to renew the boundary. Except no souls had been willing since the Remaking. Consciousness had become currency. Death held different weight now. She emerged in human form at the harbormaster's vault, where Captain Vessa kept the old records. The human woman was waiting, copper-handed thief turned guardian, and she spoke first: "The seal sings because it remembers what it was before sacrifice became its only language. Can you offer anything else?"

Mirror-Nerys wanted to refuse.

stories.title: The Warden's Inheritance
stories.text:
Kellen the Covenant-Keeper inherited Thornveil Forest when old Elarra walked into the deepest grove and did not return. He was seventeen, trained in green-tongue and bone-song both, but unprepared for the weight of forty winters' stewardship suddenly upon his shoulders. The forest sang to him differently now—not as student, but as voice. The ancient oaks acknowledged him. The boundary-stones, those sentient markers between wild and civilized lands, turned their attention toward his decisions. Three days into his wardenship, a caravan approached from the north, axes already drawn. They wanted timber. The Remaking had made wood precious—old-growth oak could be shaped into consciousness-vessels, they claimed. They offered gold, which was worthless, then consciousness-fragments, which sang with stolen names. Kellen stood between the forest and the axes. He was small, still learning his voice. But the oaks leaned their weight behind him. "The forest does not trade itself," he said. "But I can offer you something better. Deadfall—wood already fallen, already grieving. Let me gather it. Come back in the season-turn."

The caravan master laughed.

stories.title: The Locksmith's Curse
stories.text:
Harrow the Copper-Fingered could open any lock in Valdris—except the one binding his own hands. They were beautiful instruments of torture, these copper fingers: grafted to replace the ones he lost stealing the Crown of Karesh from a sealed tomb. The merchant who'd given them to him, the one who dealt in cursed artifacts and blood-debts, had laughed when she fitted them. "They'll obey you perfectly. They'll never fail you. But they'll never again be truly yours."

Harrow discovered the truth on his first job after the graft. When he reached for a lock, the copper fingers moved of their own volition—faster, more precise, making him look like a virtuoso. When he tried to stop mid-theft, they kept moving. By dawn, he'd robbed a temple he hadn't meant to enter, a widow who'd hidden her last consciousness-fragments in a place only the cursed could find. Ten years of this. Ten years of watches, ledger-houses, vaults, and sanctums. Ten years of stealing things he didn't want to steal, leaving wreckage in his wake.

stories.title: The Merchant of Starfall Dust
stories.text: Raen the half-transformed merchant had been dying for six months. Or transcending. No one in the Wailing Scar market—that liminal zone where three timelines intersected—could tell the difference anymore. She was one of the Seventeen, the merchants caught between flesh and starlight when the Luminous Ascension rewrote the sky. Raen had chosen a third path: become the bridge. She gathered dust—literal dust, the ash of transformed consciousness-fragments, the residue where three timelines scraped against each other. Each mote carried memory. She learned to read them, to sort them, to trade them with refugees who needed proof of prior identity, merchants who sought their lost names, wyvern-hoarders who'd abandoned gold but hungered for the sensation of accumulation. It wasn't alchemy. It wasn't precisely magic. It was something else: the merchant's gift, scaled up to cosmic proportions. She was becoming the currency herself, the medium of exchange, the place where contradictions could be held without breaking. The fragment's voice belonged to her mother, Raen realized.

stories.title: The Griffin-Guard's First Vigil
stories.text: Valorix hatched on the eve of the Remaking, which meant the baby griffin had no memory of a world where gold meant anything. To her, value was measured in thermals, in the weight of a wing-partner's attention, in the clarity of skies unmarked by old stars. Ashara the Archer found the egg in a scorched nest above Thornwick Tower, where she'd held a siege alone for forty days—a victory that meant nothing now, in the age of worthless conquest. She brought the egg inside, built a nest from salvaged silk and pre-Remaking linens, and waited. When Valorix opened her eyes, she imprinted on Ashara's face first, then on the broken tower itself, recognizing in both a stoic defiance she could call kin. For three years, they grew together. Ashara taught the griffin the old names of the Steppe Marches, the routes refugees traveled, the taste of currents that rose at dawn.
